- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.7) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model tends to under-forecast sharp upward moves; correct by adding 2–5% to forecast if sentiment > 0.7.
- When sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) and forecast is rising, model often over-optimistically assumes recovery; correct by subtracting 2–5% if sentiment < -0.2.
- If recent history shows a sharp spike followed by a steep drop, model often fails to anticipate the drop; apply downward correction of 3–8% in next 5–7 days if sentiment turns negative.
- If forecast is trending upward but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 7–10 days if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.
- If forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows strong upward momentum (e.g., > 3% daily gain), consider a 1–3 day lag in model’s response; adjust forecast to match true momentum if sentiment is positive and recent price is rising.
- If sentiment is high but forecast is below recent 10-day average, model underestimates sentiment-driven momentum; increase forecast by 1–3% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
- If forecast is above recent 10-day average and sentiment is low, model overestimates upside; reduce forecast by 1–3% per day until sentiment improves or price stabilizes.
